string-array.name: municipalities_array
string-array.item: Beijing is the capital of China and a municipality governed directly by the central government. It serves as a national center for politics, culture, international communication, and scientific innovation. The city brings together historic landmarks and modern urban development. The Forbidden City preserves the former imperial palace, while the Summer Palace and Temple of Heaven reflect different aspects of imperial life and ceremonial traditions. Sections of the Great Wall, including Badaling and Mutianyu, can also be visited within the municipality. Together, these places make Beijing an important destination for learning about Chinese history and cultural heritage.

Shanghai is a municipality in eastern China, located near the mouth of the Yangtze River. Its coastal position links the Yangtze River Delta with overseas markets, supporting major roles in commerce, finance, and shipping. The Huangpu River runs through the city, with the historic Bund on one side and the high-rise skyline of Pudong on the other. The Bund contains former banking and trading buildings in several architectural styles, reflecting the development of international business in Shanghai. Visitors can explore riverside promenades, traditional neighborhoods, and cultural attractions that show how the city combines its commercial past with modern urban life.

Chongqing is a municipality in Southwest China, with its central urban districts located where the Yangtze and Jialing rivers meet. Mountains, hills, valleys, and waterways shape its landscape, giving it the widely used name Mountain City. The municipality includes both major urban districts and extensive rural areas. Across the municipality, the Yangtze is joined by tributaries such as the Jialing and Wujiang. Chongqing served as the wartime capital of China during the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression. In 1997, its present status as a municipality directly under the central government was established.

Tianjin is a municipality directly administered by the central government of China. Its development has been closely connected with water transport. The opening of the Grand Canal during the Sui dynasty increased the importance of the area, and it later became a transfer point for grain and silk moving north. Tianjin Wei was established in 1404 during the Ming dynasty. After Tianjin became a treaty port in 1860, it developed into an important commercial and industrial centre in northern China. The city also played a significant role in the introduction of modern railways, telecommunications, postal services, and education.
